title: KV micro-stripe allocator with lazy relocation and batch cushioning
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Problem: continuous batching causes temporally correlated insert/delete patterns in the KV cache. Small variable-sized KV entries from multiple in-flight requests fragment GPU memory over time, increasing allocation/eviction churn and causing latency spikes and higher token cost. Existing slab and reservoir approaches reduce some fragmentation but either waste space for outliers or incur expensive compaction passes that compete with inference throughput.

Proposal: introduce a KV micro-stripe allocator with three cooperating mechanisms: micro-stripes, lazy relocation, and batch cushioning.

- Micro-stripes: divide each GPU KV arena into narrow contiguous stripes (e.g., 64–256KB) sized to fit the modal KV object distribution observed from production traces. Each stripe uses a fast bump-pointer for allocation and a small per-stripe freelist for reclaimed objects. Stripes are typed by size class at runtime; oversized objects fall back to a slow-path pool.

- Lazy relocation: instead of immediate synchronous compaction, use a cooperative background walker that migrates live entries from low-utilization stripes into hotter stripes when occupancy falls below a low-water threshold. Relocation work is scheduled by a low-priority worker running on spare CPU/GPU cycles and is bounded by a per-epoch budget to avoid interfering with inference. Relocation moves are recorded as indirection entries in a tiny per-shard forwarding table so in-flight requests see consistent reads.

- Batch cushioning: when continuous batching creates bursts of short-lived entries, allocate a small cushion region (per-stripe shadow area) reserved for burst allocations. Cushioning reduces eviction of long-lived entries during temporary load spikes by admitting short-lived entries into the cushion and letting them expire without forcing cross-stripe relocations. Cushion size is dynamically adjusted using exponential smoothing of recent burst statistics.

Design goals: reduce fragmentation and eviction churn, bound background work so latency SLOs are preserved, and keep allocation/lookup fast (O(1) common case).

Telemetry and metrics: track per-stripe occupancy distribution, reclamation rate, relocation moves/sec, average relocation latency, percentage of allocations served from cushion, eviction rate per-model, and P95/P99 token latency correlated with relocation activity. Establish baseline from prod traces: current fragmentation index and extra token cost metric.

APIs & runtime implications: no external API change. Internal runtime needs: stripe metadata in GPU memory (compact), a small indirection table per-shard (fits in L2 or pinned host memory), background relocation worker with configurable budget, and a new runtime flag to enable batch cushioning tuning.

Rollout plan: implement behind feature flag; unit and integration tests; staged Canary rollout to 5% of low-traffic hosts for 1 week, expand to 25% with perf guardrails, then full rollout. Monitor eviction rate and latency SLOs. Have immediate rollback to classic allocator on regressions.

Benchmarks: target 20–40% reduction in fragmentation index and 10–25% reduction in eviction-driven token cost on representative chat workloads with long conversation histories and high batching. Target <1% end-to-end P99 latency regression during background relocation under steady-state load.

Risks & mitigations:
- Relocation overhead interfering with inference: mitigate by strict relocation budgets and priority scheduling; can move worker to separate CPU/isolated GPU queue.
- Forwarding table adds lookup indirection: keep table tiny and cache hot entries; optimize fast-path to bypass table for non-relocated items.
- Incorrect cushion sizing could waste memory: use adaptive smoothing with conservative caps and a rollback threshold.

Testing plan: microbench suites (allocation-only, heavy-delete, bursty-batch), large-scale replay against 72-hour production trace, fault-injection for partial relocation failures, and consistency tests for indirection table under concurrent readers/writers.

Deliverables:
- RFC doc + diagrams (link: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/KV/Micro-Stripe-Allocator)
- Runtime implementation (C++/CUDA) behind flag
- Integration tests and perf harness changes (bench repo PR)
- Canary runbook and dashboard for relocation/fragmentation metrics

Success criteria: after 2 weeks of canary at 25% traffic, fragmentation index reduced by >=20% and eviction-driven token cost reduction >=10% with no P99 SLO regressions.
comments: 2026-02-21: Initial issue created. Collected allocation histograms from recent traces (chat and embed workloads). Modal KV size ~3.6KB, long tail to 128KB.
2026-02-25: Design sync with runtime team — Rafael suggested per-shard tiny forwarding table to avoid global locks. Decided to keep stripe sizing configurable per-deployment.
2026-03-01: Prototype bump-pointer stripe allocator implemented. Microbench shows 2.3x faster single-thread alloc vs baseline in small-allocation workload.

2026-03-04: Integration run with background relocation enabled showed 0.6% P99 latency increase under synthetic worst-case when relocation budget not capped. Added relocation budget limiter and retested.
2026-03-08: Verified cushion adaptive controller prevents eviction spike during 500QPS burst test. Cushion admission rate peaked at 12% of allocations and then decayed.
2026-03-10: Ready for canary PR (refs: github.com/redwood/runtime/pull/2819). Canary runbook drafted. Scheduling 5% canary on 2026-03-15.
